nameStory: The name 'speedwell' comes from an old English farewell blessing - 'speed well' meant 'may you prosper' or 'fare well on your journey.' Travelers would pick these little blue flowers as good luck charms for safe travels. The 'spiked' part refers to the tall, dense flower spikes that look like colorful exclamation points in the garden.
description: Spiked speedwell is a showy perennial wildflower that stands 1-3 feet tall with dramatic flower spikes reaching up to a foot long. These dense, bottlebrush-like spikes are packed with tiny four-petaled flowers in shades of blue, purple, pink, or white. The plant forms neat clumps with upright stems and has a tidy, garden-worthy appearance that makes it popular with both wildflower enthusiasts and pollinators. It's much more robust and eye-catching than its smaller speedwell cousins.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, spike-like clusters up to 12 inches long, packed with tiny four-petaled flowers in blue, purple, pink, or white. Each individual flower is small but the overall effect is dramatic - like a fuzzy bottlebrush.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial growing 1-3 feet tall in neat, clumping form. Stems are sturdy and hold the flower spikes well above the foliage, giving the plant an orderly, almost formal appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Leaves feel slightly rough to the touch and have small teeth along the edges, tapering to a point at the tip.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, heart-shaped seed capsules develop after flowering, splitting open to release tiny seeds. The spent flower spikes turn brown but often remain upright through fall.

habitat: Spiked speedwell is quite rare in New England, typically found in disturbed areas, old gardens, roadsides, and occasionally naturalized in meadows or field edges. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. Most sightings are likely garden escapes or remnants from old homesteads, as it's more commonly cultivated than truly wild in our region.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as neat clusters of lance-shaped leaves. Flower buds begin forming at stem tips by late spring, appearing as tight, greenish spikes.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with spectacular flower spikes in full display, typically lasting several weeks. The showy spikes are magnets for bees, butterflies, and other pollinators throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Spent flower spikes turn brown but often remain standing. Leaves may develop yellow or bronze tones before dying back, and heart-shaped seed capsules split open.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and seed heads. The plant overwinters as a basal rosette of leaves that may remain somewhat green under snow.

funFact: Spiked speedwell is so rare and special in the United Kingdom that it became a protected species in 1975 and serves as the official county flower of Montgomeryshire in Wales - making any New England sighting of this European native quite a botanical treasure hunt prize!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tall spiked flowers like lupine or blazing star, but spiked speedwell's tiny four-petaled flowers packed densely in narrow spikes are distinctive. Remember: speedwell spikes are much more densely packed and bottlebrush-like than the more open flower arrangements of similar plants.
contextualKnowledge: While many speedwells are small, weedy plants, spiked speedwell is the showboat of the genus and primarily exists in New England as a garden plant rather than a true wildflower. Its extreme rarity here (only 8 observations) means most encounters will be near old gardens or homesteads where it has escaped cultivation.
compareHints: Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters. While cousins like bird's-eye speedwell or thyme-leaved speedwell have tiny flowers in loose clusters, spiked speedwell creates dramatic, dense flower spikes that can't be missed. It's the giant among speedwell dwarfs in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
